data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The smallest positive integer is 18, derived via a complementary-remainder shortcut: the remainders 3 and 4 are complements of 2 and 3 respectively, i.e., 3 = 5\u22122 and 4 = 7\u22123; the offsets 2 and 3 form an arithmetic progression 2, 3 with common difference 1, so the solution is x = lcm(5,7) \u2212 first_offset = 35 \u2212 2 = 33... wait, but 33 mod 5 = 3 and 33 mod 7 = 5, so this fails; the correct resolution is that the offsets don't match, so we fall back to direct enumeration yielding 18.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If 33 mod 7 = 4, the constant-difference shortcut would be valid and 33 would be the answer (but 33 mod 7 = 5, so it fails)","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If a value less than 18 satisfies both congruences, 18 is not minimal","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the offset mismatch is not recognized, one might incorrectly accept 33 (the constant-difference trap)","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Step 1: Express remainders as complements: 3 = 5\u22122, 4 = 7\u22123. Step 2: The offsets 2 and 3 differ, so the constant-difference shortcut (yielding x \u2261 \u22122 mod 35, i.e., x = 33) does NOT apply \u2014 it would give x \u2261 3 mod 5 (correct) but x \u2261 5 mod 7 (wrong, since 33 mod 7 = 5, not 4). This is the constant-difference trap documented in SCR_002. Step 3: Fall back to direct enumeration: x \u2261 3 mod 5 gives 3, 8, 13, 18; check mod 7: 3 mod 7 = 3 (fail), 8 mod 7 = 1 (fail), 13 mod 7 = 6 (fail), 18 mod 7 = 4 (pass). So 18 is minimal.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
